markdown:
## Do you need your own OAuth app?

If your AI agent’s users must connect their GitHub account, this guide covers registering your own GitHub OAuth app. Whether any alternative setup path exists for this flow is not documented. An individual can create and register an OAuth app under a personal account or under any organization they administer.

## Before you start

- You need a GitHub account. To register under an organization, you need administrative access to that organization.
- Decide on an application name, a homepage URL, and an authorization callback URL.
- The application description is optional, but users will see it if you provide one.
- You can enter up to 10 callback URLs; additional URLs are added with **Add callback URL**.

## Step-by-step setup

1. Go to the OAuth app registration page: `https://github.com/settings/applications/new`.
2. The documented setup path lives under **Developer settings** in the left sidebar.
3. Enter the required fields: application name, homepage URL, and authorization callback URL.
4. Optionally enter an application description.
5. Add callback URLs as needed, up to the documented limit of 10, using **Add callback URL**.

After registration, every OAuth app is assigned a unique Client ID and Client Secret. Treat the secret as confidential.

## Scopes

Scopes limit OAuth token access. They do not grant any additional permission beyond what the user already has. The documented granular scopes include:

- `repo`
- `public_repo`
- `user`, `read:user`, `user:email`, `user:follow`
- `org`, `admin:org`, `write:org`, `read:org`
- `admin:repo_hook`
- `gist`
- `workflow`
- `codespace`
- `packages`
- `delete_repo`
- `notifications`
- `project`
- `offline_access`

The `offline_access` scope requests an expiring access token plus a refresh token, even if the OAuth app is not configured to use expiring tokens. Use it to test and gradually roll out support for expiring tokens. The `X-OAuth-Scopes` and `X-Accepted-OAuth-Scopes` response headers reveal a token’s granted scopes.

## Approval and review

No app review, verification, or approval process is documented in the sources reviewed. This appears to be self-serve. Because no review or verification step appears, there is no documented period in which the app is treated as unverified. Setup time is estimated at about 5–10 minutes from the documented steps; the provider does not publish a duration.

## What the agent can do vs. what you must do

An agent can research the public documentation, draft the app settings, redirect URIs, and scopes, write the authorization and token-exchange code, and keep credentials in server-side environment variables. It cannot create the provider account, click through the provider console, accept terms on your behalf, or submit an approval.

You must create the OAuth app, copy the client ID and secret into your deployment, and own the provider relationship. No provider review or verification step appears in the sources reviewed; confirm that with the provider before launch. The remaining work is console setup and credential handling.

This guide was produced from public documentation; no provider account was used and no approval was submitted.

## What this guide does not know

- The provider does not publish a setup duration; the 5–10 minute figure is an estimate based on a self-serve form with no documented prerequisite artifacts.
- No review, verification, or approval step is documented, so this guide cannot say whether any internal review occurs before the app becomes usable.
- The experience of an unverified or pending app is not documented.
- No troubleshooting, error, or rollback guidance is documented for this flow.
- Anything outside the registration fields and scopes listed above is not covered.
